opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, it's great to be here.

For me it came from a couple of threads coming together. Personally, I'd noticed how much of my day, and honestly most people's days, is spent doing small, tedious things on the web: checking whether something has changed, filling out the same forms, comparing options across a bunch of tabs, keeping an eye on things you care about. None of it is hard, but it adds up, and it pulls your attention away from what actually matters. So there was a very human motivation: can we give people back some of that time and mental bandwidth?

On the technical side, it felt like the moment had arrived. For a long time, the idea of an assistant that could reliably operate on the open web was more aspiration than reality. The models just weren't good enough at reasoning, planning, or understanding what's on a page. That's changed a lot. Multimodal models can now look at a webpage and make sense of it, they can follow multi-step instructions, and they can recover when something unexpected happens, at least some of the time. That "some of the time" is the interesting part. It means the capability is there, but there's still a lot of hard work to make it robust and trustworthy enough that people will actually rely on it.

That gap is what makes it a great opportunity. The web is messy. Sites change, layouts are inconsistent, things break, and the long tail is enormous. You can't solve that with a demo; you have to deal with reliability, evaluation, latency, cost, and just as importantly, the interaction design. When should the agent check in with you? How much autonomy do you give it? How do you build trust over time? Those are deep research questions, but they're also very product-shaped questions, and I find that combination really exciting.

And finally, the web is where so much of the world's information and services live. If you can build agents that navigate it well on someone's behalf, that's a really general capability. It's not one narrow use case; it's potentially a new layer between people and everything they do online. That felt like the right place to put my energy.

r001.rationale: The response says models were not previously good enough and that reliability still needs work, but it does not state that simply running GPT in a loop was insufficient.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare the timeline for reliable web agents with the timeline for reliable robotics.

r003.rationale: It calls web agents a promising opportunity and describes remaining research questions, but does not clearly say the gap is tractable enough for a research-oriented team to make substantial progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it came from a few different threads kind of converging at once. For a long time, a lot of my work was in vision and language, grounding, and then generative AI, and the question underlying a lot of it was really about getting AI systems to be useful to people in the actual contexts they live and work in. And when I stepped back and asked where that happens today, the answer is overwhelmingly the browser. That's where people do their work, manage their lives, buy things, fill out forms, coordinate with other people. So if you care about AI that actually does things for people rather than just talks about them, the web is sort of the natural surface.

The second thread was that the models had gotten good enough that it stopped feeling like a research curiosity and started feeling like an engineering problem that was within reach. A couple of years ago, a web agent would work on a demo and fall over the moment you changed the website. Now the reasoning and the multimodal understanding are strong enough that you can actually have a model look at a page, understand what it's trying to accomplish, recover from mistakes, and keep going. That shift from "sometimes works" to "works often enough that you can build on it" is the moment where I think it gets interesting.

And honestly, the third piece was that it's a really hard problem in a way that I find fun. The web is adversarial, it's messy, it's constantly changing, it was designed for humans and not for machines. There's no clean API. So you're dealing with long-horizon planning, with partial observability, with the question of when the agent should act versus ask, with safety and trust, all at once. It touches almost every open question in the field, but in a setting where you can measure whether you actually got the task done. That combination of practical impact and deep technical challenge was pretty irresistible to me.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier agents failed when websites changed, but does not state that simply running GPT in a loop was insufficient.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the timeline for reliable web agents with the timeline for reliable robotics.

r003.rationale: The response calls the problem within reach and technically challenging, but does not identify the remaining capability gap as tractable for a research-oriented team to make substantial progress.

astra-6.text:
What appealed to me was the combination of a really broad interface and a concrete technical challenge. So much of what we do happens through a browser. If an agent can operate in that environment, there’s a wide range of tasks it could potentially help with, without needing a separate integration for every one.

But getting there requires much more than understanding a request. The agent has to interpret what’s on the page, decide what to do, observe what changed, and recover when something doesn’t work. It’s this continuous loop of perception, reasoning, and action. And you have a fairly concrete way to ask whether it succeeded: did it actually accomplish what the user wanted? That combination made it feel like a compelling area to work on.

sol-6.1.text:
What appealed to me was the combination of a very general interface and a very concrete way to be useful. So much of what we do happens through a browser. If an agent can operate in that environment, you don’t need to build a separate integration for every task you might want help with.

And technically, it brings together a lot of interesting challenges. You have to understand what’s on the page, connect that to the user’s intent, decide what action to take, and then look at what happened and adjust. It’s not just producing an answer; it’s this ongoing loop of perception, reasoning, and action. That felt like a compelling place to work on turning model capabilities into something that can actually get things done.
